w: Founded in 1910 as a natural history society, this state body became ground zero for the Leakeys' human-origins research and now holds Fort Jesus, Lamu Old Town and the Sacred Mijikenda Kaya Forests among its charges - plus 7.5 million specimens stacked in the East African Herbarium.
s: Where the Leakeys rewrote human origins
_facts: Originated 1910 under East Africa Natural History Society
Louis and Richard Leakey directed human-origins study
Oversees Fort Jesus, Lamu Old Town, Sacred Mijikenda Kaya Forests (UNESCO sites)
East African Herbarium holds 7.5 million specimens

w: Jomo Kenyatta opened this lakeside park in 1969; the Moi regime later broke up a land-rights protest here by force, and by 2021 it was fenced off in razor wire over a tree-felling scandal a court had to halt. It reopened in 2024 - now a weekend skate spot with an artificial lake for company.
s: Skateboards roll where protests once got crushed
_facts: Opened by Jomo Kenyatta 23 May 1969
Site of Moi-era violent break-up of land-grabbing protest
2021 renovation halted by court over environmental concerns, park fenced/closed
Reopened 30 March 2024 by Governor Sakaja
Popular skateboarding spot with artificial lake

n: Cathedral Basilica of the Holy Family
w: The 1904 original - just 300-400 seats - was the first stone building Nairobi ever raised. Its 1960s replacement, seat of the Archdiocese, was blessed open in July 1963 and earned basilica status in 1982: a colonial-era parish that outgrew itself twice over.
s: Nairobi's first stone building, reborn as a basilica
_facts: 1904 original church was Nairobi's first stone building, 300-400 seats
Current church built 1960-1963, opened 6 July 1963
Seat of the Archdiocese of Nairobi
Designated a basilica in 1982

w: Opened in 1902 by Mayence Bent when Nairobi was a railway halt, the Stanley became the default meeting point for anyone heading on safari. Suites are named for guests who passed through - Karen Blixen, Hemingway, the Duke of Windsor - and the Thorn Tree Cafe once served as the city's message board, pinned to an acacia.
s: The safari crowd's living room since 1902
_facts: Established 1902 by Mayence Bent, Nairobi's first luxury hotel
Traditional meeting place for safari-goers since early 1900s
Suites named for Duke of Windsor, Karen Blixen, Hemingway; Churchill Ballroom
Thorn Tree Cafe named for acacia used as a message depot

w: Opened in 1971 on the old East African Railways site, this museum kept its rail link live so exhibits can still be shuttled for upkeep. One locomotive, No. 2301, played a supporting role in the 1985 film Out of Africa; three working steam engines sit under cover, viewable only by appointment.
s: Steam engines that once starred in Out of Africa
_facts: Opened 1971 by East African Railways and Harbours Corporation
Operated by Kenya Railways, maintains rail connection
Locomotive 301 (2301) used in 1985 film Out of Africa
Three operational steam locomotives, viewing by appointment only

w: A state-run tourist village in Langata built around bomas - traditional homesteads - representing Kenya's many communities, paired with one of Africa's largest auditoriums for the dance performances staged there. A crash course in the country's cultural range, ten minutes from the CBD.
s: Every Kenyan tribe's homestead, under one roof
_facts: Tourist village in Langata, Nairobi
Displays traditional villages of Kenyan tribes ('bomas' = homesteads)
Home to one of Africa's largest auditoriums
About 10km from Nairobi CBD; state corporation

w: Set up by an act of parliament in 1965 inside a former Kenya Commercial Bank building on Moi Avenue, the archive holds 40,000 volumes of the country's paper trail. Tucked inside is the Murumbi Gallery, a trove of African artefacts gathered across the 19th century - history filed behind a banking facade.
_facts: Established 1965 by Act of Parliament, on Moi Avenue
Building originally housed Kenya Commercial Bank
Holds 40,000 volumes
Houses the Murumbi Gallery of 19th-century African artefacts

w: Fenced on three sides since 1946, with its open southern edge left for wildlife to move onto the Kitengela plains, this park somehow keeps a full savanna cast - rhino, lion, migrating herds - within sight of the capital's skyline. One of Kenya's most successful rhino sanctuaries, against the odds.
s: Lions and rhinos, seven kilometres from downtown
_facts: Established 1946, about 7km south of Nairobi
Fenced on three sides; open southern boundary lets wildlife migrate to Kitengela plains
Large varied wildlife population despite small size
One of Kenya's most successful rhinoceros sanctuaries

w: Founded in 1902 and built between 1925 and 1933 on Banda Street, Jamia has been the centre of Muslim religious life in Kenya through the colonial years and after - hosting Friday prayers, a newsletter, and its own TV station today. Marble halls in the heart of the CBD, still the address for the ummah's business.
_facts: Founded by Syed Maulana Abdullah Shah in 1902
Constructed 1925-1933 on Banda Street, Nairobi CBD
Extended with modern wing in 1998, houses library, hall, newsletter and Horizon TV
Central hub for Muslim community, Friday prayers

w: An open-air Langata institution built around an all-you-can-eat meat buffet, Carnivore was once famous for its game meat until Kenya's 2004 hunting ban ended that chapter. It swapped species, not popularity, and remains one of the city's stock tourist pilgrimages.
_facts: Open-air restaurant in Langata suburb
All-you-can-eat meat buffet specialty
Famous for game meat until Kenya's 2004 ban on game meat sale
Remains a popular tourist destination

w: Jock Leslie-Melville - a Kenyan grandson of a Scottish earl - and his wife Betty started this sanctuary in 1979 after capturing two baby giraffes on their Lang'ata property, breeding Rothschild's giraffes for reintroduction to the wild. Visitors now feed them by hand from a raised platform, warthogs included underfoot.
s: Feed a Rothschild's giraffe from a treehouse deck
_facts: Started 1979 by Jock Leslie-Melville and wife Betty on their Lang'ata property
Protects vulnerable Rothschild's giraffe
Breeding programme has reintroduced pairs into national parks
Visitor Centre established by 1983; feeding platform main attraction; warthogs also roam the site

w: A.M. Jeevanjee, an Asian-born entrepreneur, donated this CBD garden to the city in trust for its people - making it, by local telling, the only park in Nairobi that belongs directly to residents rather than the state. A patch of shade held in common, in the middle of downtown traffic.
s: The only park Nairobians actually own
_facts: Open garden in Nairobi's Central Business District
Founded by A.M. Jeevanjee, an Asian-born entrepreneur
Donated to the people of Nairobi, held in trust as a resting area
Said to be the only park in the city directly owned by the people
